Step-by-step instructions on how to perform an activity with clearly defined roles and responsibilities.

To provide clear and unambiguous guidelines on process work steps. Procedures help with:

  • Implementation of consistent work methods
  • Compliance and quality assurance to evaluate whether processes are being performed to defined standards
  • Compliance with company policies and industry regulations
  • Appropriate monitoring and control performance against procedures, roles, and responsibilities

Lack of procedural documentation could lead to:

  • Failure to comply with required policies, standards, or regulations
  • Lack of consistency in how a procedure is performed which may lead to issues with efficiency and/or quality
  • Ambiguity in roles and responsibilities
  • Lack of understanding complexity and level of effort required for a given procedure, resulting in potential staffing issues

Procedures should at a minimum contain the following components:

  • Procedure Name: name of the procedure and the supporting business unit/function to which it applies
  • Procedure Summary: overview of the scope and objective of the procedure
  • Procedure: detailed description of the steps required to be taken by the business group to execute the procedures:
    • What is required to be performed?
    • How is it accomplished?
    • Who are the responsible parties/groups performing the activities?
    • What is the timing and frequency of these activities?
    • What are the other key controls in place?
    • What systems are to be used or what reports are to be generated?

They may additionally contain the following:

  • Related Policies: information about related policies governing the specific procedure (if available)
  • Business Unit/Function Area Procedures Information: information about the owner, effective date, and reference to specific policy numbers (if available)
  • Supervision/Oversight: general description of how the procedure will be supervised, any oversight processes (i.e., management reports, review of trading accounts, etc.) and the function responsible for the oversight
  • Escalation: description of how issues, including general exception requests, should be escalated and the specific committee or position to which they should be escalated
  • Monitoring: description of the monitoring processes in place to determine that procedures are being followed (i.e., audits, compliance reviews, routine surveillance, etc.)
  • Recordkeeping: identifies specific records, including systems that will be created and retained to implement the procedure, including supervision, escalation, and monitoring. This section should, at a minimum:
    • Address each type of record referenced in the corresponding procedure
    • Define where records are kept
    • Outline the time frame for which records are kept (generally three years onsite and another three years which may be offsite, provided the records are readily accessible).

Procedures can be represented in the following forms of documentation. The representation options listed below are typically combined in a single document:

  • High-level process flows
  • Detailed process narratives or steps
  • Supporting checklists
